title: Nuts with the most omega-3

seo.title: Nuts with the most omega-3: ranked by serving
seo.meta_description: Walnuts stand far above other common nuts for omega-3, with about 2.57 g of ALA per 1 oz serving. Most other nuts provide much less.
seo.search_intent: Find which nuts provide the most omega-3 and understand how plant ALA differs from fish EPA and DHA.

excerpt: Walnuts are by far the common nut with the most omega-3: a 1 oz (28 g) serving provides about 2.57 g of alpha-linolenic acid (ALA). Pecans, pistachios, almonds, hazelnuts, and cashews provide much smaller amounts. ALA is a plant omega-3 and is not nutritionally identical to the EPA and DHA found in fish.
content_html:
If omega-3 is the specific reason you are choosing a nut, the comparison is unusually clear: walnuts are in a different category from the rest. The gap is not a rounding error. It is large enough to change the practical choice.

The key distinction is that the omega-3 in nuts is primarily alpha-linolenic acid (ALA). Fatty fish, by contrast, provides EPA and DHA. All three are omega-3 fats, but they are not metabolically interchangeable gram for gram.

Omega-3 ALA per 1 oz serving

The table uses a 1 oz (28 g) serving so the numbers reflect a realistic snack portion rather than 100 g of a calorie-dense food.

NutALA per 1 oz
Walnuts2.57 g
Pecans0.28 g
Pistachios0.08 g
Hazelnuts0.02 g
Cashews0.02 g
Almonds0.00–0.01 g

The meaningful gap is between walnuts and everything else. A serving of walnuts provides roughly nine times as much ALA as pecans and far more than pistachios, almonds, hazelnuts, or cashews.

Why walnuts are different

Walnuts have a fatty-acid profile that is more heavily weighted toward polyunsaturated fat than many other nuts. Almonds, hazelnuts, and macadamias are richer in monounsaturated fat, while walnuts contain a notable amount of ALA.

That does not make other nuts nutritionally inferior. Almonds may contribute more vitamin E, pistachios have their own micronutrient profile, and all nuts can fit into a healthy dietary pattern. It simply means that for the narrow question of plant omega-3, walnuts are the clear standout.

ALA is not the same as EPA and DHA

The body can convert some ALA into EPA and then DHA, but the conversion is limited. So 2.57 g of ALA from walnuts should not be described as equivalent to 2.57 g of EPA plus DHA from fish.

The NIH identifies ALA as an essential fatty acid that must come from food. Walnuts, flax, chia, and certain oils can therefore make meaningful contributions to plant omega-3 intake, especially in diets that contain little or no fish.

A normal serving already provides a substantial amount

U.S. adequate intake values for ALA are 1.6 g per day for adult men and 1.1 g for adult women. A 1 oz serving of walnuts contains about 2.57 g, which puts the food-level number into perspective.

There is no need to use a 100 g portion to make walnuts look impressive. A realistic serving already contains a substantial amount of ALA, while also keeping the calorie context visible.

What about peanuts?

Peanuts are botanically legumes, even though they are eaten like nuts. Their ALA content is low compared with walnuts, so including them does not change the practical conclusion.

The useful takeaway

If you want the highest omega-3 option among common nuts, choose walnuts. If you specifically want EPA and DHA, however, the relevant foods are fatty fish, seafood, and certain fortified foods or supplements rather than nuts.

faq.question: Which nut has the most omega-3?
faq.answer: Walnuts. A 1 oz (28 g) serving provides about 2.57 g of ALA, far more than pecans, pistachios, almonds, hazelnuts, or cashews.

faq.question: Is walnut omega-3 the same as salmon omega-3?
faq.answer: No. Walnuts mainly provide ALA, while salmon provides EPA and DHA. The body can convert some ALA, but the conversion is limited.

faq.question: How many walnuts do I need for omega-3?
faq.answer: A standard 1 oz serving already provides about 2.57 g of ALA.
